title: PJM's new firm-capacity rule for AI data centers takes effect — no generation, first in line for curtailment
subtitle: The largest US grid operator now requires any 50-MW-plus load — the size class every hyperscaler AI campus lands in — to bring its own generation or accept being cut first when the system is short.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: PJM Interconnection's new 'Large Load' framework, approved by the PJM board on July 27 and filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission with a requested effective date of July 31, is now live across the largest US grid. Any customer with 50 megawatts or more of cumulative peak demand at a single site within a one-mile radius counts as a Large Load — a threshold that captures essentially every hyperscaler AI training or inference campus. Starting June 1, 2027, any new Large Load that has not secured its own generating capacity or otherwise locked in firm supply will be first in line for curtailment when PJM's resource margins get tight. Firm grid service, in other words, is no longer the default for a new AI campus in PJM's 13-state footprint.

The mechanism is a direct response to how sharply AI has bent PJM's demand curve. PJM's most recent capacity auction cleared at a record — data center loads accounted for roughly $6.3 billion of the auction cost, according to PJM's independent market monitor — and the operator's forward projections show existing generation retiring faster than replacements are entering the interconnection queue. FERC's July directive to PJM to create transparent rules for co-located data-center loads gave the grid operator regulatory cover to move fast; the filed rule creates a category of customers whose service quality is explicitly conditional, in exchange for keeping the interconnection door open at all.

For hyperscalers this changes the site-selection calculus in PJM. Bring-your-own-generation was already common for the largest planned campuses — Meta's El Paso deal with BlackRock, Microsoft's various nuclear PPAs, Amazon's Talen deal at Susquehanna — but the new rule pushes it from a competitive edge to a baseline requirement for any project that wants firm service from day one. Expect a wave of behind-the-meter gas turbines, small modular reactor PPAs, and long-duration battery deals filed alongside site-selection announcements. The rule also creates a strong incentive to develop outside PJM entirely, in ERCOT (Texas) or MISO (Upper Midwest), which is likely to accelerate the geographic dispersion of AI infrastructure buildout already underway.

For learners: the AI capital-expenditure story is often told through GPU counts and data-center square footage, but the binding constraint over the next 24 months is electricity — specifically firm, dispatchable electricity in interconnections that have real growth headroom. PJM's rule is a bellwether. Watch whether MISO, SPP, and ERCOT adopt similar frameworks; watch which hyperscalers announce co-located generation deals alongside their next big campus; and watch the small modular reactor filings at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Those three signals will tell you more about where AI infrastructure actually lands than any leaderboard will.
